title: The Fourth Patriarch Instructs Farong
author: Zhanran (annotated)
excerpt: Bǎo (protection): cutting off thought and deliberation. Rèn (spontaneity): letting the mind be free, without love or hate, grasping or rejecting.

inline.s: The original text is taken from the Compendium of Five Lamps (Wudeng Huiyuan)
Bǎo (protection): cutting off thought and deliberation.
Rèn (spontaneity): letting the mind be free, without love or hate, grasping or rejecting.
[Cutting off thought and deliberation] Not a single thought arises. [Letting the mind be free] Letting the mind come and go freely, without defilement and without admixture. The Sixth Patriarch said:
“Let the six consciousnesses
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness)
go out through the six gates
(the six sense faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind)
, and among the six sense objects
(form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas)
remain undefiled and unadulterated, coming and going freely, penetrating and unimpeded.”
(The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch) Confucius said:
“To follow the heart’s desires without overstepping the measure.”
The Analects
“Wei Zheng”)

The Confucian practice also has these two stages, protection (bǎo) and spontaneity (rèn). The stage of protection is “restraining the self and returning to propriety” — concretely, the “four prohibitions”: “Do not look at what is contrary to propriety; do not listen to what is contrary to propriety; do not speak what is contrary to propriety; do not act contrary to propriety.” (The Analects

“Yan Yuan”) The stage of spontaneity is: “to follow the heart’s desires without overstepping the measure.” Here the “measure” is the Confucian “propriety” (lǐ). [Propriety] Propriety is the regulating pattern (norm) of a person’s conduct. Now, while a person lives in the world, he is stained by ordinary dust; amid the gaudy scenes of the world, most take fame and gain as their desire, and their hearts are moved by them. When the heart moves, evil arises. An unrectified heart gives rise to unrectified thoughts, and its conduct is likewise unrectified. Therefore one regulates it with propriety and harmonizes it with music, guiding the unrectified heart and rectifying the unrectified conduct. With body and mind made upright, one reaches the upright path of the human way. [Restraining the self and returning to propriety] To constrain oneself so that every matter accords with “propriety.” “Restrain” (kè) means to check and control.
Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou
was
a native of Yanling in Runzhou
His surname was Wei. At nineteen he had thoroughly studied the classics and histories
Later he read the great Prajñā scriptures and awakened to true emptiness
One day he suddenly sighed and said:
The worldly classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma
The right contemplation of prajñā is the boat that crosses out of the world
Thereupon he retired to Mount Mao, took a teacher, and had his head shaved
Afterwards he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Monastery on Mount Niutou, where there was the marvel of a hundred birds carrying flowers in their beaks
(a wondrous sign of a hundred birds carrying flowers as offerings, from which one can see that
Farong’s attainment at this time was already extraordinary
[Farong (
)] The founder of the Niutou (Ox Head) school.
In the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch
Chan Master Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school
observed the signs from afar and knew that on that mountain there was an extraordinary person, so he personally
(in person)
went to seek him out
He asked a monk of the monastery:
Is there anyone of the Way here
a person who has attained the Way
The monk said:
Which of us who have left home is
nǎ, “which”
not a person of the Way
The Patriarch said:
Which one is the person of the Way
Well then, which one is the person who has attained the Way — you tell me.
The monk had no answer
the monk was left speechless
Another monk said:
About ten li into these mountains there is a “Lazy Rong” who does not rise when he sees people, nor even join his palms — might he be a person of the Way
might he
be a person who has attained the Way)
The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master
Farong
sitting upright at ease
just as before
, paying him no attention at all
not the least bit minding him
The Patriarch asked:
What are you doing here
The Master said:
Contemplating the mind
(this
shows that Farong attained what is later called “cutting off thought and deliberation” through contemplating the mind
The Patriarch said:
Who is it that contemplates
who is doing the contemplating
And what is the mind
what is the mind
The Master had no answer, so he rose and bowed
and said:
Where does the great worthy dwell
The Patriarch said:
This poor monk has no fixed abode
I have no fixed place to stay
, now east, now west
The Master said:
Do you know Chan Master Daoxin
The Patriarch said:
Why do you ask about him
The Master said:
I have long admired his virtue
I have long admired his virtuous manner
, and hope to pay my respects
I hope to be able to call on him
The Patriarch said:
Chan Master Daoxin — that poor monk is me
The Master said:
Why have you come down here
The Patriarch said:
I have come especially to visit you
Is there some other place to rest
to stay
The Master pointed behind him and said:
There is another small hut
He then led the Patriarch to the hut

[Contemplating the mind] To observe one’s own mind. The mind is the master of all dharmas, and not a single thing is outside the mind; therefore to observe one’s own mind is to observe everything. Within the three realms, the mind is the master; one who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation. Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Treatise on Breaking Through Forms says: “The single method of contemplating the mind encompasses all dharmas and is the most direct and essential.”
Going around the hut, one saw only such creatures as tigers and wolves, so the Patriarch raised both hands in a gesture of fright
(the Fourth Patriarch raised both hands in a gesture of alarm and fear)
The Master said:
So you still have this in you
The Patriarch said:
What is this
The Master was speechless
After a short while
(after
a moment
, the Patriarch wrote on the rock where the Master sat in meditation
in sitting meditation
a single
Buddha
character; the Master, seeing it, was alarmed
his hair stood on end: how could one write the character “Buddha” where one sits!
The Patriarch said:
So you still have this in you
The Master did not understand, and so bowed his head and begged for the essential truth.
The Patriarch said: ‘The hundred thousand Dharma gates all return to the square inch
the mind

; the wondrous virtues numerous as the Ganges’ sands all rest in the mind-source. All gates of precepts, of samādhi, of wisdom, and all spiritual powers and transformations are complete within you, not apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are from the beginning empty and quiescent; all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There are no three realms to leave, no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans are equal in nature and in form. The great Way is empty
(xū, the archaic form of “void”)
and vast,
cutting off thought and deliberation
. This Dharma
(cutting off thought and deliberation)
you have now attained
you
have now
achieved cutting off thought and deliberation — the work of protection is accomplished
, and it lacks
same as “lacking”
nothing; how does it differ from the Buddha? There is no other Dharma besides.
You need only let your mind be free
now begin the work of spontaneity
— letting the mind be free)

, and do not engage in contemplation, nor still the mind, nor arouse greed or anger, nor harbor worry; vast and unobstructed, go freely wherever you will. Do no wholesome deeds, do no evil deeds. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, whatever meets the eye, whatever circumstance you meet, it is all the wondrous functioning of the Buddha — joyful and without care; therefore it is called “Buddha.”’
[Mind-source] The mind is the source of all dharmas, hence it is called the mind-source. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says: “When a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it
when the delusion ceases, the mind-source is empty and quiescent

all virtues are complete, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.” The Great Calm and Contemplation says: “Sit cross-legged with hands folded, lips sealed and tongue stilled, and contemplate the true mark

Once the mind-source comes to rest, the whole Dharma realm is equally quiescent.” It also says: “If one wishes to illuminate and know, one must know the mind-source. When the mind-source is non-dual, all dharmas are alike as empty space.” [Non-human] Refers to the non-human devas, nāgas, and the eight kinds of beings, as well as yakṣas, evil ghosts, asuras, hell beings, and so on. It is also used generally as a term for ghosts and spirits. [Protection and spontaneity] Protection and spontaneity are the two stages of
cleansing
away residual
habitual tendencies
after seeing one’s nature. “Protection” is to do one’s utmost to care for the sacred embryo (the initially awakened self-nature)
so
that it
is kept from
greed, anger, and delusion’s
harm
, thereby accomplishing the first two of the four kinds of forbearance (the forbearance of subjugation and the forbearance of gentleness)

; “Spontaneity” means that after the sacred embryo has grown to maturity, it follows circumstances and functions naturally, undergoing further tempering amid favorable and adverse circumstances, in order to accomplish the latter two of the four kinds of forbearance
(the forbearance of no-birth and the forbearance of quiescence)
. Farong accomplished “protection” through cutting off thought and deliberation; now the Fourth Patriarch wants him to let his mind be free, in order to accomplish “spontaneity.”

[The four kinds of forbearance] The forbearance of subjugation, the forbearance of gentleness, the forbearance of no-birth, and the forbearance of quiescence. The forbearance of subjugation is when a practitioner at the initial stage, wishing to endure favorable and adverse circumstances (
without giving rise to greed, anger, and delusion)

, must first subdue and tame his mind; the forbearance of gentleness is when, having tamed the mind for a long time, one encounters circumstances and conditions and is able to endure naturally (without giving rise to greed, anger, and delusion) without forcing or suppressing — at this time the mind is gentle, good, and compliant; the forbearance of no-birth is for a person of the holy stages, who has realized that all dharmas are from the beginning unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and lack self-nature, and are empty in their very essence; therefore, within the Dharma of no self-nature, his forbearing mind is unmoved, and he personally realizes no-birth; the forbearance of quiescence is for a sage of the fruition stage, who has thoroughly realized the state of nirvāṇa’s quiescence, where both the marks of movement and stillness accord with suchness. [Suchness] The self-nature state in which inverted discrimination does not arise. Because it is the true suchness (the true mark of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom of principle, it is called “suchness” (rú rú). [Contemplation] The practice of contemplating the mind.
The Master said: ‘Since the mind is complete
(the mind
being
complete with
all things
, what is the Buddha? What is the mind?’ The Patriarch said:
If it were not the mind, you would not ask about the Buddha; to ask about the Buddha is none other than the mind

[If it were not the mind, you would not ask about the Buddha; to ask about the Buddha is none other than the mind] The meaning is: the mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the mind. That is, as is commonly said: the mind is precisely the Buddha.
The Master said:
Since you do not permit contemplative practice,
when a circumstance arises, how does the mind deal with it
The Patriarch said: ‘Circumstances have no good or bad; good and bad arise from the mind.
If the mind does not forcibly assign names
(if the mind does not insist on discriminating “good” and “bad”)
, how can deluded feelings arise
(therefore, not forcibly assigning names is the way to deal with it “when a circumstance arises”)
When deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind freely knows all. You need only follow the mind in freedom
when a circumstance arises, merely do not forcibly assign names
, with no further remedial measures,
and this is called the abiding Dharma body
this is the state attained through accomplished spontaneity
, without change or variation
no longer subject to the birth-and-death of transformation
. I received from Master Can
(càn,
the Third Patriarch Sengcan of the Chan school
the Dharma gate of sudden awakening, and now transmit it to you. Receive my words with care; dwell only on this mountain. Hereafter there will be five persons who attain
it
hereafter there will be people who comprehend
your Chan Dharma — an allusion to the five persons from the second patriarch of the Niutou school, Zhiyan, to the sixth patriarch, Huisi)
, to carry on
your profound teaching
(to carry on your holy and virtuous teaching)
.’ The Patriarch finished transmitting the Dharma
(the Fourth Patriarch finished transmitting
the Dharma
, and then returned to Twin Peaks
(Twin Peaks Mountain in Huangmei, Hubei)
to live out his final years

[Circumstances have no good or bad] Circumstances have no “good” or “not good.” Here “bad” (chǒu) means “not good.” [Freedom] A mind free from the bondage of afflictions, penetrating and unimpeded, is called freedom (zìzài). The Lotus Sūtra

“Introduction” chapter says: “Exhausting all the bonds of existence, the mind attains freedom.” [Bonds of existence] “Existence” is the retributive fruit of birth and death; “bonds” are the afflictions that can attract this retribution. Afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion can bind people and keep them dwelling within the realm of birth and death, unable to leave; hence they are called “bonds of existence.”
[Two kinds of death] The birth-and-death of division and the birth-and-death of transformation.

[Birth-and-death of division] Among sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the response to wholesome and unwholesome karma, their lifespans all have limits, and their bodies all have separate segments; hence their birth and death is called the “birth-and-death of division.” One who ends the birth-and-death of division escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Birth-and-death of transformation] The sages among the three vehicles (the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas) have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, and ended the birth-and-death of division. In the course of cultivating the Way, as confusion gradually dies away and realization gradually increases, this migration between confusion and awakening differs from period to period. Moving from an earlier period into a later period is just like undergoing birth and death once; hence it is called the “birth-and-death of transformation.” One who ends the birth-and-death of transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question: Circumstances clearly do have good and bad (good and not good). Why does the Fourth Patriarch say that “circumstances have no good or bad”?
Answer: “Circumstances have no good or bad” is said with regard to the true mark of all dharmas (for details, see
“The True Mark of All Dharmas”

). In the dream of ignorance, the myriad phenomena all carry various discriminations, and so there is the distinction of good and bad; but they are all illusory and unreal — matters within a dream. In actual fact, they do not exist at all, so where could there be any discrimination? Therefore the Heart Sūtra says:
“All these dharmas are empty in their marks — not born, not ceasing, not defiled, not pure, not increasing, not decreasing.”
(In translation: all these dharmas are illusory marks; in reality there is no birth or cessation, defilement or purity, increase or decrease.) For the annotation, see
“The Heart Sūtra, Finely Explained”
Summary:
Farong’s process of cultivation can be divided into two great stages: protection (bǎo) and spontaneity (rèn).
Protection: cutting off thought and deliberation — that is, what the Diamond Sūtra calls:
“The mind should not abide in form to give rise to thoughts, nor abide in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas to give rise to thoughts.”
This is what the Chan school calls the great death, attained through contemplating the mind.
Spontaneity: letting the mind move freely without defilement — that is, what the Diamond Sūtra calls:
“One should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.”
This is what the Chan school calls the great life — reviving again after the absolute.
Chan Master Daochong (a Linji school monk of the Song dynasty) said:
“On the cliff’s edge
(cutting off thought and deliberation)
let go your hands
(no further remedial measures)
, and dare to accept it yourself
(dare to move from protection into spontaneity)
; revive again after the absolute
(and you will emerge from the great death into the great life)
, there is no deceiving you
(I will certainly not deceive you)
. Brothers, if you can truly, at the place of no breath
(cutting off thought and deliberation)
, revive after the absolute
(follow the mind in freedom, abiding nowhere)
, and at ease
(in the ordinary way)
bring it forth into use,
without falling into the old rut of right and wrong, gain and loss
, then you can leave the monastery and enter the villages.”
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daochong)
[Old rut (
kē jiù

)] A stale pattern. [Leaving the monastery and entering the villages] Meaning that one can go out from the mountain into the towns to deliver and transform sentient beings. [Monastery] A place where monks dwell together, hence a temple. [Villages] Here referring to villages and towns, because they are established on the basis of mutual protection (bǎo).
